title: The Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol for Tea Efflux Appliances (HTCPCP-TEA)
summary: This is an April 1st joke RFC. It extends the humorous Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol so networked pots can brew tea in all its variety. It is not a serious specification.

eli5.summary: This is a joke document about telling a teapot over the Internet to make tea, which is silly but written like a real rulebook.

questions: what is the hyper text coffee pot control protocol
what is the message/teapot media type
how do you brew tea over http
subtitle: An April 1st joke extension that teaches networked coffee pots to brew tea.

tldr.problem: The joke says HTCPCP has no way to brew tea, and only lets networked teapots refuse coffee.
tldr.mechanism: Clients send BREW with the content type message/teapot, the pot answers a request to / with an Alternates header listing teas, and the client then picks a tea URI.
tldr.outcome: It is an April 1st humor document that updates RFC 2324 and is not a real specification.

today: RFC 7168 is an April 1st Informational document that updates RFC 2324 and has not been obsoleted. It is humor, not a real specification.

sections.title: The Joke: Tea for HTCPCP
sections.content: RFC 7168 is an April 1st joke document, dated 1 April 2014. It extends the Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol of RFC 2324, which it notes has no provision for networked tea, other than that teapots should not answer requests for coffee. The extension covers control of devices that make tea.
sections.eli5: The coffee pot rule book had nothing for tea. This adds a chapter for teapots.

sections.title: Choosing and Brewing Tea
sections.content:
Control is through BREW requests, and POST is treated the same but remains deprecated. A TEA-capable pot receiving a BREW of content type message/teapot MUST respond according to the URI requested. For the URI /, brewing does not start. Instead the pot MUST send an Alternates header (RFC 2295) listing the available teas, such as /darjeeling, /earl-grey and /peppermint. Clients MUST check it and use a specific URI next. A request to / with message/coffeepot SHOULD get the same answer.

For a specific variety, pots follow base HTCPCP and SHOULD stop at the recommended brewing strength, perhaps measured by opacity. Clients SHOULD send a BREW with the body stop to end brewing. If it arrives early the pot MUST abort and serve weaker tea. Without it the proportion of tea to water may invert and be reported as negative strength.
sections.eli5: First the pot shows a menu of teas. You pick one, and tell it "stop" when the tea looks strong enough.

sections.title: Header, Codes and Media Type
sections.content:
The Accept-Additions header gains a sugar-type of Sugar, Xylitol or Stevia. The RFC warns that too much Sugar may make the request exceed the transport segment size and cause fragmentation.

The pot should answer 300 when brewing has not started. It MAY answer 403 when requested additions offend a consensus of drinkers about that tea. A pot that cannot brew coffee may return 503 for temporary unavailability or 418 to show it is permanently a teapot. A new media type, message/teapot, MUST be the Content-Type when tea is requested.
sections.eli5: The pot has a few polite answers: here is the menu, no you cannot put that in your tea, and I am a teapot.

sections.title: Environment and Security
sections.content:
If a BREW with message/coffeepot reaches a pot that can make coffee, base HTCPCP behavior applies and coffee is brewed. A client that did not want it SHOULD send stop, which wastes coffee. Asking for message/teapot first avoids that waste.

On security, electric pots are not near fire, so no firewalls are needed. Coal-fired pots and electrically heated kettles should not share a network, so pots do not call kettles darkened or smoke driven.
sections.eli5: Ask for tea first so no coffee gets poured by mistake. Keep fire-heated pots away from electric kettles.
